blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Shape a story through exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution; build suspense by withholding and then releasing key information.

blocks.heading: Freytag’s Pyramid
blocks.text: Freytag’s Pyramid is the story arc in five stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Exposition establishes the situation and the people before the trouble starts — it gives the reader the ordinary that the rest of the story will disrupt. Rising action complicates it. The climax is the story’s turning point, where the conflict meets its decisive moment. Falling action carries the consequence. The resolution shows what changed and closes what the exposition opened. The imaginative/descriptive task is one of Section B’s categories, set at 600–900 words and twenty-five marks, and the pyramid is the plan a story variant starts from.

blocks.heading: Planning a story on the pyramid
blocks.text: Planning a 600–900-word story on the pyramid means one conflict, few characters and one setting — the arc has room for nothing else. Choose one conflict a reader can hold in one sentence. Give it two or three people, and one place. Mark the exposition (about 100 words), the rising action (about 300), the climax (about 150, slowed), the falling action and resolution (about 200). A crowded arc is no arc: every extra plot is the main plot’s thief.

blocks.heading: Contained plot against chain of events
blocks.text: A contained plot is one conflict followed to its consequence; a chain of events is several conflicts interrupting each other, and the reader is left holding none of them. "The storm took the roof, then the teacher left, then the dog ran away, then the town voted" is four stories in one, each robbed of its ending; "the storm took the roof, and the family had to decide what the house still was" is one story with its decision to travel to. The word count does the arguing: 600–900 words holds one arc, properly.

blocks.heading: Overloading the plot
blocks.text: The error is the plot overloaded with events and characters, or built on events that cannot be believed: it loses the reader’s trust and the story’s shape at once. In 600–900 words, one believable conflict beats three inventions, because the reader’s trust is the story’s currency — spent on the third coincidence, there is none left for the climax. The companion error is dialogue that runs on, carries no story and is badly punctuated: speech earns its lines by moving the conflict or showing a person, and it is punctuated and paragraphed by its own rules — new speaker, new paragraph, punctuation inside the marks.

blocks.heading: Worked example: withholding in practice
blocks.text: A story opens with a narrator locking a door and refusing to say what is behind it — the withholding starts in the first line. The rising action lets three details of what is behind it escape (a sound, a smell, a name said once) without releasing the fact. The climax releases it — one sentence, the withheld thing said at last — and the story’s power is the gap between the reader’s three guesses and the one truth. The withheld thing is a debt the story repays, and the repayment lands harder for the wait: that is the mechanism of suspense, used on purpose.

blocks.heading: Slowing the pace at the climax
blocks.text: Slowing the pace at the climax — more detail of smaller time-steps, the moment broken into beats — stretches the decisive seconds so the reader lives in them rather than passing through: the rope is taken in three movements, and each movement gets its own sentence. The technique is the opposite of summary: the climax is the one place where fewer events per line makes the scene faster, because the reader stops counting events and starts standing in them.

blocks.heading: Missing the named effect
blocks.text: A story that never creates the effect the question names — drama, suspense, mystery, calm — has answered a different question: the named effect is part of the task, and the writing is judged by it. The check is to name the effect at the top of the plan and test each section against it: if the task asks for suspense, the plan withholds something; if it asks for calm, no section ends on a cliff. A well-written story that creates the wrong effect is a poorer fit to the task than a plainer one that creates the right one.
